title: Monster-in-Law
full_review:
After a 15-year hiatus, Jane Fonda returns to the big screen in the lightweight comedy "Monster-in-Law" (New Line). It wasn't worth the wait.

Directed by Robert Luketic, the movie isn't particularly awful; it's just not all that good.

Jennifer Lopez co-stars as Charlotte "Charlie" Cantilini, a job-juggling temp and aspiring fashion designer who is looking for Mr. Right. Ten minutes into the film, she finds him in the person of handsome doctor Kevin Fields (Michael Vartan), a "dream guy" with a nightmare mom lurking at the other end of the apron string.

Fonda plays Viola, Kevin's rich, batty, three-times divorced and borderline-alcoholic mom, a Barbara Walters-like diva who is axed for a younger face after a distinguished broadcast career.

During the taping of her final show, Viola experiences an on-air meltdown, attacking her interview subject -- a vapid Brittany Spears clone who thinks that Roe vs. Wade was a boxing match (one of two abortion references in the script).

After a stint in rehab, Viola returns home only to have her tenuous serenity -- and sobriety -- tested when Kevin proposes to Charlie in front of her.

Fearing that she will lose her son as she did her job -- to another woman -- Viola, who doesn't think that Charlie is good enough for Kevin, determines to derail the impending nuptials.

When humiliation fails, she tries to scare off her prospective daughter-in-law by smothering her with sweetness, even offering to help plan the big day.

Feigning mental duress, Viola contrives to move in with the couple, who are already living together, so she can ratchet up her sabotage efforts.

But the claws really come out when Charlie gets wise to Viola's scheme and gives her a taste of her own Machiavellian medicine, escalating the catfight.

Apart from the couple's problematic living arrangement and the mean-spirited tone of some of the humor (at one point Viola contemplates spiking Charlie's food with a potentially toxic allergen), "Monster-in-Law" is more forgettable than objectionable.

The film has a few laughs, but by striving for breezy romance the potential for a first-rate black comedy (a la "War of the Roses") is wasted.

Fonda's unhinged and intentionally over-the-top performance is the best thing about the movie and makes it more entertaining than it deserves to be. Though, after 15 years, is this mediocre fare really the best script she could find?

As for her sparring partner, Lopez mugs through most of the film, recycling bits of her "Wedding Planner" and "Maid in Manhattan" roles. Vartan is so bland that you wonder what either woman sees in him.

Wise-cracking Wanda Sykes, who plays Viola's sassy personal assistant, Ruby, gets the wittiest zingers, humorously inverting the old Hollywood "subservient black maid" stereotype.

Screen veteran Elaine Stritch has a funny cameo late in the game. Adam Scott and Annie Parisse play Charlie's perfunctory best friends -- gay and straight, respectively -- but serve little purpose beyond one-dimensional sounding boards for Charlie.

The film contains some sexual situations and humor, including several crude gestures, some comic violence, and sporadic crass language and profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
